explanation: X86-64 architecture defines specific conventions for passing floating-point arguments to functions and returning floating-point values. Understanding these conventions is crucial for writing correct and efficient system-level code, ensuring proper hardware-software interaction within the processor's register set and memory management.
syntax: Floating-point arguments are passed in XMM registers (%xmm0-%xmm7) in the order they are listed in the function declaration.  Up to eight arguments can be passed this way; additional arguments are passed on the stack.  A function returning a floating-point value does so in %xmm0. All XMM registers are caller-saved.
code_example: double f1(int x, double y, long z);
/* x in %edi, y in %xmm0, z in %rsi */
example_explanation: The example shows a function declaration `f1`.  According to the x86-64 floating-point conventions, the integer argument `x` is passed in the general-purpose register %edi, the double-precision floating-point argument `y` is passed in the XMM register %xmm0, and the long integer argument `z` is passed in the general-purpose register %rsi. This illustrates how argument passing uses different registers based on data type and order, demonstrating the interplay between general-purpose registers and XMM floating-point registers in the x86-64 architecture.

extraction_metadata.source: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition)
